summary: A catalog of the available X.500 directory service implementations and their capabilities. X.500 is an OSI standard for directories, and this informational document helps people see which implementations existed. It was replaced by RFC 1632.

eli5.summary: A shopping list of the different programs that could run a big electronic phone book called X.500. It tells you what each one can do.

questions: what is a directory system agent
what are the components of x.500
subtitle: A reference list of X.500 directory software implementations and their capabilities.

tldr.problem: X.500 is a complex OSI-based directory service protocol with many implementations from different vendors. People choosing or deploying X.500 needed to know what implementations existed, what they could do, and how to obtain them.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC catalogs commercially available and freely available X.500 implementations (Directory System Agents, Directory User Agents, and client applications) organized by keywords describing their features, platforms, and capabilities.
tldr.outcome: The document provided a helpful snapshot of the X.500 landscape in 1992. However, X.500 adoption remained limited in the broader Internet, and LDAP later became the dominant directory service protocol. The RFC was replaced by RFC 1632.

facts.label: Platforms covered
facts.value: Unix, VMS, Macintosh, various vendor systems

today: RFC 1292 is Informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 1632. X.500 itself has remained a niche technology, primarily used in specialized domains like telecommunications and public key infrastructure. LDAP became the dominant directory service protocol for Internet use because of its simplicity and TCP/IP integration. Modern directory systems often support LDAP (or LDAP-compatible APIs) rather than native X.500.

sections.title: What Is X.500 and Why This Catalog
sections.content:
X.500 is an international standard for a distributed directory service developed by CCITT (now ITU). It allows organizations to store and look up information about people and resources in a hierarchical, federated network of directory servers. The Information Services Infrastructure (DISI) Working Group recognized that as X.500 pilot projects grew (such as the White Pages Pilot Project and the NIST/GSA Pilot), people needed to know what implementations were available.

This RFC aims to lower the barrier to X.500 adoption by providing an accessible source of information about existing implementations. The catalog includes commercial products and freely available offerings, describing both the server components (Directory System Agents) and client components (Directory User Agents and applications) that people could deploy. The descriptions were written by implementors and vendors themselves, reviewed for readability but not verified by the working group.
sections.eli5: X.500 is a big electronic phone book spread across many computers. This document lists all the different programs you could use to run or search that phone book.

sections.title: X.500 Components and Concepts
sections.content:
X.500 has several components. A Directory System Agent (DSA) is a server that holds part of the directory and responds to queries. A Directory User Agent (DUA) is a client-side program that allows users to search the directory or an application-level client that connects to a DUA. A Directory Information Base (DIB) is the database of directory information.

X.500 implementations use protocols called DAP (Directory Access Protocol) and DSP (Directory System Protocol) defined in the OSI X.500 specification. The networking layer can be built on various transports: CLNP (OSI's native network protocol), X.25 (a packet-switched data service), RFC-1006 (X.500 over TCP/IP), or pure OSI transport protocols.

The catalog indexes implementations by functional categories. Availability categories include: Available via FTP or FTAM, Commercially Available, Free, or Source Available. Implementation types distinguish DSA-only implementations, DUA-only implementations, or combined DSA/DUA systems. Networking environment describes which protocol stack and transport are used. Pilot connectivity indicates whether the implementation can connect to active X.500 pilot projects.
sections.eli5: X.500 has different pieces: servers that store the data, clients that search it, and different ways to connect them all together. Implementations mix and match these pieces in different ways.

sections.title: The Catalog Organization and Keywords
sections.content:
The RFC defines keywords to describe implementations, organized into several categories:

  • Availability: How you can get the software (FTP, commercial purchase, free, with source code available)
  • Implementation Type: Whether it is a DSA alone, DUA alone, or combined; whether it includes an API; whether it is a lightweight DUA client
  • Networking Environment: What protocols it uses (CLNP, X.25, RFC-1006, generic OSI transport)
  • Pilot Connectivity: Whether the DUA can connect to directory pilots and whether the DSA is connected to the global directory
  • Platform: What hardware it runs on (Sun, HP, DEC, Macintosh, IBM, etc.)
  • Operating System: Unix variants, VMS, etc.
  • Dependencies: Whether ISODE (Open Systems Interconnection Developments) is required, whether it uses X Window System

Each implementation is listed alphabetically with its full description, which includes: name, vendor, last modified date, keywords, abstract, completeness against standards, interoperability notes, pilot connectivity level, known bugs, caveats, networking environments supported, hardware and software requirements, and availability information.
sections.eli5: The catalog organizes implementations by asking simple questions: Can you get it free or buy it? Does it run on your computer? Does it use which networking method? This helps you find implementations that fit your needs.

sections.title: Notable Implementations
sections.content:
The RFC catalogs numerous implementations from vendors including Touch Communications (Alliance OSI X.500), Custos, HP, Bull, Siemens, and others. Examples include:

  • Alliance OSI X.500 (Touch Communications): A commercially available DSA/DUA implementation with an API, available on multiple platforms (HP, MIPS, Sun, Macintosh, IBM) using RFC-1006 or OSI transport
  • QUIPU: A free, open-source implementation that includes both DSA and DUA, available via FTP with source code, runs on Unix systems
  • VMS-ISODE: A free implementation for DEC VMS systems with DSA and DUA
  • DIXIE: A free DUA with an X Window System interface
  • Mac-ISODE: Brings ISODE to Apple Macintosh platforms

The implementations vary widely in completeness, with some claiming full X.500 compliance and others implementing limited functionality intentionally for ease of use. Some require ISODE (a port of OSI software) as a dependency.
sections.eli5: Different companies and groups wrote X.500 software. Some sold it, some gave it away free. Some worked on many platforms, some only on specific ones. The catalog helps you find which one suits your situation.

sections.title: The X.500 Vision and Its Limitations
sections.content:
X.500 was envisioned as a global, hierarchical directory service where organizations would operate DSAs that federated into a unified directory tree. Pilot projects in North America and Europe attempted to demonstrate this. The catalog reflects optimism about X.500's potential: the DISI Working Group solicited input from the X.500 community to help enable its continued growth.

However, X.500's complexity (as an OSI protocol requiring heavyweight implementations and specific networking infrastructure) and the simultaneous rise of TCP/IP as the dominant Internet protocol made adoption difficult. LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol), a simpler TCP/IP-based directory protocol, eventually became more popular. RFC 1292 was replaced by RFC 1632, and X.500 remained primarily used in specialized environments (telecommunications, public key infrastructure) rather than becoming the Internet's universal directory.
sections.eli5: X.500 was supposed to be the Internet's phone book, but it turned out to be too complicated. A simpler system called LDAP became more popular instead.
